aireadiness.plain: AI readiness is how prepared a company is to use AI well: whether it has usable data, people with time to own the work, a stable process to improve, a platform to run it on, and a way to manage the risks. Use-case prioritisation is the job of choosing which AI ideas to build first. A use case is one specific task AI could help with, such as 'sort incoming claims emails into 12 queues', with a named user, a volume and a pain. You collect many use cases, score them all the same way, and pick one or two for a first pilot. The result is a short AI roadmap: a plan of what gets built, in what order, by whom, and how success is measured.
aireadiness.analogy: It is like a builder visiting a house before a renovation. First they check the foundations, wiring and budget (readiness). Then they list everything the owners want, from a new kitchen to a hot tub, price each wish and pick the job that adds the most value without the house falling down (prioritisation).
aireadiness.why: Many customers arrive saying 'we need to do AI' without a specific problem. If an FDE starts building the most exciting idea, the pilot often stalls in week three because the data is locked away, no one owns the result, or legal will never approve it. A clear readiness check and a scored list let the FDE steer the customer to a first win, which is what keeps the engagement and the budget alive.

subtopics.title: Assessing readiness: five dimensions
subtopics.body:
Readiness is not one number. Check five dimensions, each with a few plain questions.

Data: does the information the AI needs exist, is it digital, and can you get access to it within weeks, not months? A company may have ten years of claims records, but if they sit in scanned PDFs on a file share with no index, that is a data gap. People: is there an executive sponsor (the senior person who pays for and defends the project), a product owner who makes day-to-day decisions, and users who have time to test? Process: is the workflow stable and understood? If every branch handles claims differently, the AI will learn a mess. Platform: where would the AI run? Some customers allow only one cloud, some ban sending data to outside model providers, some have no way to deploy new services without a six-month approval. Risk: what could go wrong for customers, staff, the law or the brand, and who signs off on that risk?

Score each dimension red, amber or green, and write one sentence of evidence for each. Evidence matters more than the colour: 'Green: claims system has a read-only API, IT confirmed access on 3 March' is useful, while 'Green: data is fine' is not.

A readiness check is not a reason to say no. Its job is to find gaps early so you can plan them: an amber data rating becomes a task on the roadmap with an owner and a date. This work overlaps with Discovery and with Compliance; link to those topics for interview technique and privacy law.
subtopics.example: Quillmoor Insurance (made up, 1,800 staff) asks for 'an AI strategy'. In a one-week check the FDE rates data amber (claims emails are archived, but attachments are scanned images), people green (the claims director will sponsor, a team lead will own it), process amber (three regional teams triage differently), platform green (approved cloud tenant, model provider under contract) and risk amber (emails contain health details). The summary goes to the sponsor with three gap actions, each owned.

subtopics.title: Running a use-case discovery workshop
subtopics.body:
A use-case workshop turns vague interest into a list of specific, comparable ideas. It usually takes two to three hours with six to twelve people.

Invite the people who do the work, not only managers. A claims handler knows which emails take the most time; a director may not. Also invite someone from IT and, if possible, someone from risk or legal, so bad ideas are caught in the room.

A simple agenda has four parts. First, ten minutes on what AI is good and bad at, with two examples from the customer's industry, so ideas are realistic. Second, map the work: ask each team to list their most repetitive, text-heavy or judgement-light tasks and the hours they take. Third, generate ideas: each person writes ideas on cards, one per card, in the form 'Help [user] do [task] so that [outcome]'. Fourth, cluster duplicates and fill in the facts for each card: who uses it, how often (volume), how long it takes today (baseline), and where the data lives.

Edge cases: if one senior person dominates, collect cards silently first, then discuss. If people suggest vague ideas ('use AI for customer service'), ask 'what exactly would the user do differently on Monday?'. If the room has no ideas, bring three examples from similar companies as starters. End by explaining what happens next: you will score the ideas and come back in a week with a recommendation.
subtopics.example: At Quillmoor the workshop has 9 people from claims, underwriting, IT and compliance. They produce 31 cards, which cluster into 14 ideas. The top card reads: 'Help claims handlers sort incoming emails into the right queue so that urgent claims are seen the same day.' Facts added: 2,600 emails a day, about 90 seconds each to read and route, data in the shared mailbox.

0:00  What AI can and cannot do here   (10 min, 2 industry examples)
0:10  Map the work                      (30 min)
      - list repetitive, text-heavy tasks and hours per week
0:40  Silent idea cards                 (20 min)
      - 'Help [user] do [task] so that [outcome]', one per card
1:00  Cluster and remove duplicates     (20 min)
1:20  Fill in facts for each idea       (40 min)
      - user, volume per week, minutes today, data source, owner
2:00  Quick risk check with legal / IT  (20 min)
2:20  Next steps                        (10 min)
      - we score all ideas and return with a recommendation in 1 week

subtopics.title: Scoring use cases on the same scale
subtopics.body:
Once you have a list, score every idea with the same criteria so the choice is fair and defensible. Four criteria cover most cases.

Value: how much time, money or risk does it save, and for how many people? Use the workshop facts: volume times minutes saved gives hours per year. Feasibility: how hard is it to build with today's tools? Reading and sorting text is feasible; making final legal decisions is not. Data availability: can you get enough real, representative examples, with permission? Risk: what happens when the AI is wrong, and how bad is it? A wrong email route is cheap to fix; a wrong fraud accusation is not.

Use a 1 to 5 scale with a written meaning for each number, for example value 5 means 'more than 5,000 hours a year saved'. Without anchors, people score by feeling. Then combine the scores with weights. Value often gets the biggest weight, but data and risk act as gates: an idea with data scored 1 cannot be first, however valuable it looks.

Keep the scoring sheet visible to the customer. When the loudest executive's favourite idea lands in fourth place, the sheet explains why in a way that is about facts, not people. Invite the sponsor to change a weight if they disagree; this often starts a useful conversation about what the company really cares about.

Edge case: ties. When two ideas score almost the same, prefer the one with a clearer baseline number, because you will need to prove improvement later.
subtopics.example: The code scores five Quillmoor ideas. Claims email triage wins at 4.20. Broker quote extraction scores well but is flagged because its data (quotes in many broker formats) is rated 2. Fraud flagging has the highest value but high risk and low feasibility, so it is not a first pilot.
subtopics.code:
# Score candidate use cases the same way (1 = poor, 5 = great)
# risk is 1 (low) to 5 (high), so we flip it: safety = 6 - risk
WEIGHTS = {"value": 0.40, "feasibility": 0.25, "data": 0.20, "safety": 0.15}

ideas = [
    # name,                       value, feasibility, data, risk
    ("Claims email triage",           4, 4, 5, 2),
    ("Adjuster note summaries",       3, 5, 4, 2),
    ("Fraud flagging",                5, 2, 3, 5),
    ("Policy Q&A chatbot for public", 4, 3, 3, 4),
    ("Broker quote extraction",       4, 3, 2, 2),
]

def score(value, feas, data, risk):
    parts = {"value": value, "feasibility": feas, "data": data, "safety": 6 - risk}
    return round(sum(WEIGHTS[k] * v for k, v in parts.items()), 2)

ranked = sorted(ideas, key=lambda i: score(*i[1:]), reverse=True)
for name, *s in ranked:
    gate = "" if s[2] >= 3 else "  (blocked: data)"   # data below 3 = not ready yet
    print(f"{score(*s):.2f}  {name}{gate}")

# Output:
# -> 4.20  Claims email triage
# -> 3.85  Adjuster note summaries
# -> 3.35  Broker quote extraction  (blocked: data)
# -> 3.25  Fraud flagging
# -> 3.25  Policy Q&A chatbot for public

subtopics.title: The 2x2 matrix and choosing a first pilot
subtopics.body:
A 2x2 matrix is a simple picture that puts every idea on two axes, usually value (up) and effort (right). It splits ideas into four boxes. Quick wins: high value, low effort. Big bets: high value, high effort. Fillers: low value, low effort. Avoid: low value, high effort. Executives like the picture because they can see the whole list at once.

The first pilot should almost always be a quick win. A pilot is a small, time-boxed build with real users that proves value, usually 6 to 12 weeks. For a first pilot, you want a result that arrives fast and is easy to measure, so the customer trusts the team and funds the next step. A big bet is better as the second or third project, once the platform, access and trust exist.

Before you commit, run a final checklist on the chosen idea. Many ideas look like quick wins on paper but fail one of these checks, so treat each item as a must.

Edge cases: sometimes the sponsor insists on a big bet first. You can agree to it while proposing a quick win in parallel, or you can cut the big bet into a first slice (for example, 'flag suspicious claims for review' instead of 'detect fraud'). The Proof of concept topic covers how to run the pilot once it is chosen.
subtopics.example: On Quillmoor's matrix, claims email triage and adjuster note summaries are quick wins. The FDE recommends email triage first because it has a clean baseline (90 seconds per email, 2,600 a day) and a willing team lead, and keeps note summaries as the second pilot.
checklist: The idea is in the quick-win box
A named product owner has time each week
Real data is accessible within 2 weeks
There is a baseline number to beat
A wrong answer is cheap to catch and fix
Legal or risk has no blocking objection
Success can be measured within 8 weeks
subtopics.code:
# Place each idea on a value / effort 2x2 (scores 1 to 5, midline at 3)
ideas = {
    "Claims email triage":      (4, 2),   # (value, effort)
    "Adjuster note summaries":  (3, 1),
    "Fraud flagging":           (5, 4),
    "Public policy chatbot":    (4, 3),
    "Office party planner":     (1, 1),
}

def quadrant(value, effort):
    high_value = value >= 3
    low_effort = effort < 3          # an effort of exactly 3 counts as high
    if high_value and low_effort:  return "Quick win: pilot first"
    if high_value:                 return "Big bet: plan for later"
    if low_effort:                 return "Filler: only if spare time"
    return "Avoid"

for name, (v, e) in ideas.items():
    print(f"{name:25} {quadrant(v, e)}")

# Output:
# -> Claims email triage       Quick win: pilot first
# -> Adjuster note summaries   Quick win: pilot first
# -> Fraud flagging            Big bet: plan for later
# -> Public policy chatbot     Big bet: plan for later
# -> Office party planner      Filler: only if spare time

subtopics.title: Build, buy or configure for each use case
subtopics.body:
For every idea on the list, decide how it should be delivered. There are three options.

Configure means turning on or setting up a feature in a tool the customer already owns. Many office suites, CRMs and help-desk tools now include AI features such as summaries or drafting. Configuring is fast and cheap, but you get only what the vendor offers. Buy means purchasing a specialised product, such as a dedicated document-extraction tool. It is quicker than building and comes with support, but it adds a vendor, a contract and a security review. Build means writing a custom system, for example calling a model API with the customer's own data, prompts and rules. It fits unique workflows and deep integrations, but the customer must run and maintain it after you leave.

A useful rule: configure if a good-enough feature already exists, buy if the problem is common across companies, build if the workflow is unique or the integration is the hard part. An honest FDE recommends configure or buy when they fit, even if their own company sells build work. This honesty earns trust for the ideas that truly need building.

Edge case: 'configure' can hide costs. Licences for AI add-ons are often per user per month, which adds up for thousands of staff, and data may leave the region. Check pricing and data handling before you call it the cheap option.
subtopics.example: At Quillmoor, meeting summaries for managers are served by configuring the AI feature in their existing office suite. Broker quote extraction is a common problem, so they evaluate two document-AI products. Claims email triage needs rules tied to Quillmoor's own 12 queues and its claims system, so it is a build.

subtopics.title: Writing the AI roadmap the sponsor signs
subtopics.body:
The roadmap is the short document that turns all this work into a decision. The sponsor signs it, which means they agree to fund the first pilot, provide people and access, and accept the stated risks.

Keep it to two or three pages. It should contain: the goal in business terms (for example 'reduce claims backlog by half'), the readiness summary with gaps and owners, the ranked use-case list with scores, the first pilot with its success criteria and baseline, the next two or three ideas with rough timing, and what is explicitly out of scope. Add a decision section at the end with the sponsor's name and date.

Success criteria must be measurable. 'Better triage' is not a criterion. 'At least 85% of emails routed to the correct queue, measured on 500 emails labelled by team leads, and average handling time under 30 seconds' is. Link each criterion to the baseline you collected in the workshop.

Plan in stages, not in a big list. A typical first year has one pilot in the first quarter, a production rollout and a second pilot in the second quarter, and scaling in the second half. Tie later stages to results: 'Start pilot 2 only if pilot 1 meets its criteria.' This protects both sides from committing to ten projects at once. Review the roadmap every quarter, since data access, tools and priorities change.
subtopics.example: Quillmoor's roadmap, two pages, is signed by the claims director on 28 March. Pilot 1 is claims email triage, 8 weeks, success at 85% correct routing on a 500-email test set. Pilot 2, adjuster note summaries, starts in Q3 if pilot 1 passes. Fraud flagging is listed as 'explore in 2027 after data work'. The ai-readiness template in this atlas has the full layout.

glossary: AI readiness
How prepared an organisation is to use AI, judged on data, people, process, platform and risk.
Use case
One specific task AI could help with, with a named user, volume and pain.
Executive sponsor
The senior person who funds the project, removes blockers and signs key decisions.
Product owner
The customer person who makes day-to-day decisions about what the system should do.
Baseline
The measured performance today, such as minutes per email, that the pilot must beat.
Scoring rubric
A written scale that says what each score means, so different people score the same way.
2x2 matrix
A chart that places ideas on two axes, such as value and effort, to show quick wins.
Quick win
An idea with high value and low effort, usually the best first pilot.
Pilot
A small, time-boxed build with real users that proves an idea works before full rollout.
Build, buy or configure
The choice between custom software, a purchased product, or a feature in a tool already owned.
AI roadmap
A short staged plan of which AI projects happen in what order, with success criteria, signed by the sponsor.
practice: Pick an organisation you know (a school, shop or club). Rate it red, amber or green on the five readiness dimensions and write one sentence of evidence for each.
Write eight use-case cards in the form 'Help [user] do [task] so that [outcome]' for that organisation, each with a volume and minutes per task.
Copy the scoring code, change the weights so risk counts double, and explain in two sentences how the ranking changes and whether that makes sense.
Draw a 2x2 of your eight ideas and pick a first pilot. Run it through the pilot checklist and note any item it fails.
Stretch: write a two-page roadmap with goal, readiness summary, pilot success criteria with a baseline, two later phases with conditions, and an out-of-scope list.

golive.plain: Going live means moving a system from testing into daily use by real people on real data. Implementation is the set of steps that gets you there. User acceptance testing (UAT) is when the customer's own users try the system on realistic tasks and formally agree it is fit to use. Cutover is the planned moment you switch from the old way of working to the new system, often over a weekend or evening. A go/no-go meeting is the short decision meeting just before cutover where named people say yes or no based on agreed criteria. Hypercare is the first weeks after go-live when the team watches closely and fixes problems fast.
golive.analogy: It is like opening a new restaurant. You do test dinners for friends (UAT), move the stock from the old kitchen on a quiet night (migration and cutover), have a final check the afternoon before opening (go/no-go), and keep the head chef on the floor every night for the first two weeks (hypercare).
golive.why: Many AI projects work in a demo and then fail in the last mile because nobody planned the data move, the customer's change approval, or what to do if things break on day one. FDEs are often the person who writes the cutover plan and chairs the go/no-go meeting. A calm, well-planned go-live is one of the strongest signals of trust a customer will remember.

subtopics.title: Environments and who owns each
subtopics.body:
An environment is a separate copy of the system with its own servers, settings and data. Most customers have at least four. Development (dev) is where engineers build and break things. Test, sometimes called QA, is where features are checked against test cases. Staging, also called pre-production, is meant to be a close copy of production, with the same settings, network rules and integrations, so a release that works there should work in production. Production (prod) is the live system real users depend on.

For each environment, find out three things early: who owns it (who can grant access and approve changes), what data it may hold, and how code gets there. Customers often allow only masked or synthetic data outside production, meaning names and account numbers are replaced with fake values. That rule matters for AI projects, because evaluating a model on fake data can hide real problems. Agree a plan for how you will test on realistic data, for example a masked copy of 2,000 real records approved by the privacy team.

Common edge cases: staging is not really like production (a different identity provider, a smaller database, no connection to the real email server), so tests pass in staging and fail on go-live day. Or the vendor team has admin rights in dev but no access at all to production, which is normal and healthy; plan for someone on the customer side to run the production steps while you guide them. Write all of this in a one-page environment map at the start of the project.
subtopics.example: Castlemere Water (made up, a regional utility) is going live with an AI assistant that routes customer emails. Dev is in the FDE team's own cloud account with synthetic emails. Test and staging sit in Castlemere's cloud tenant, owned by their platform team, with masked emails. Production is owned by IT operations; only two Castlemere engineers can deploy there, during agreed windows.

subtopics.title: Data migration, backfill and reconciliation
subtopics.body:
Data migration means moving existing records from an old system into the new one. Backfill means processing historical data so the new system has a useful history on day one, for example classifying the last six months of emails so dashboards are not empty. Both can go wrong silently: rows get dropped, dates shift time zone, text loses accents, or a status value changes case.

The defence is the dry run and reconciliation. A dry run is a full practice migration into staging, timed and repeated until it is boring. Reconciliation means proving the target matches the source with numbers, not by looking at a few rows. Compare the row count per category (for example per status), sums of important numbers (totals of amounts), and a list of IDs that are missing on either side. Then pick 20 random records and check them field by field with a customer user.

Time the dry run. If the migration takes nine hours and the cutover window is six, you need to change the plan (migrate history the week before and only the last day's changes during cutover, called a delta load). Write the reconciliation queries once and run them after every dry run and during the real cutover, so everyone knows what 'good' looks like.

Edge cases: records that change while you migrate, duplicates in the source that the new system rejects, and fields with no clear mapping. Log every rejected row in a file with a reason; never let rows disappear quietly.
subtopics.example: In Castlemere's second dry run, the code below shows one closed case missing and a status whose case changed from 'pending' to 'Pending'. Comparing case-insensitively makes the pending counts match, and the missing ID 4 leads to a rejected-row log: the record had a blank customer ID, which the new system requires. The fix goes into the mapping rules before dry run three.
subtopics.code:
# Reconcile a dry-run migration: compare counts and totals per status
source = [  # rows exported from the old case system
    {"id": 1, "status": "open", "amount": 120.0},
    {"id": 2, "status": "open", "amount": 80.5},
    {"id": 3, "status": "closed", "amount": 42.0},
    {"id": 4, "status": "closed", "amount": 10.0},
    {"id": 5, "status": "pending", "amount": 300.0},
]
target = [  # the same rows after loading into the new system
    {"id": 1, "status": "open", "amount": 120.0},
    {"id": 2, "status": "open", "amount": 80.5},
    {"id": 3, "status": "closed", "amount": 42.0},
    {"id": 5, "status": "Pending", "amount": 300.0},  # case changed on load
]

def summary(rows):
    out = {}
    for r in rows:
        key = r["status"].lower()          # compare case-insensitively
        cnt, tot = out.get(key, (0, 0.0))
        out[key] = (cnt + 1, tot + r["amount"])
    return out

s, t = summary(source), summary(target)
for key in sorted(s):
    ok = "OK" if s[key] == t.get(key) else "MISMATCH"
    print(key, s[key], t.get(key), ok)
missing = {r["id"] for r in source} - {r["id"] for r in target}
print("missing ids:", sorted(missing))

# Output:
# -> closed (2, 52.0) (1, 42.0) MISMATCH
# -> open (2, 200.5) (2, 200.5) OK
# -> pending (1, 300.0) (1, 300.0) OK
# -> missing ids: [4]

subtopics.title: User acceptance testing: scripts, sign-off, defects
subtopics.body:
User acceptance testing (UAT) is when business users, not engineers, test the system on realistic tasks and decide whether it is acceptable. It checks that the system does the job people need, which unit tests and evals cannot fully prove.

Start with UAT scripts. Each script is a short scenario with numbered steps, the data to use and the expected result, written in the user's language: 'Open email 17 (a burst pipe report). Expected: routed to Emergencies within 1 minute, with priority High.' Cover the common cases, the important rare cases and the failure paths, such as what the user sees when the AI is unsure. For an AI system, add a batch test: users review 200 real items and mark each output right or wrong, because single scripted examples do not show accuracy.

Testers record pass or fail and raise a defect for each failure. A defect is a logged problem with steps to reproduce, severity and an owner. Triage defects daily: decide severity, who fixes it, and whether it blocks go-live. Agree the exit criteria before UAT starts, for example: all critical scripts pass, no open critical or high defects, medium defects have a workaround and a fix date, batch accuracy at least 90%.

Sign-off is a named business owner stating in writing that the system meets the criteria. Without it, go-live becomes a matter of opinion. Edge case: testers who are too busy. Book their time in their managers' calendars two weeks ahead.
subtopics.example: Castlemere runs UAT for five days with six customer-service agents. They run 24 scripts and review 250 real emails. Two high defects appear (outage emails mentioning 'no water' routed to Billing) and are fixed and retested by day four. Batch accuracy is 93%. The customer-service manager signs the UAT sheet on Friday.

subtopics.title: Change control: the CAB and release windows
subtopics.body:
Large customers do not let anyone change production whenever they like. Change control is the process for proposing, approving and recording changes to live systems. Many organisations follow ITIL, a widely used set of IT service practices, which groups changes into three kinds. Standard changes are low-risk, pre-approved and repeatable, such as restarting a service. Normal changes need review and approval. Emergency changes fix urgent problems and use a fast approval path.

Normal changes usually go to a Change Advisory Board (CAB), a regular meeting (often weekly) where IT, security and business representatives review upcoming changes. You submit a change request, sometimes called an RFC, with what is changing, why, the risk, the test evidence, the implementation steps, the rollback plan and who will be on hand. The CAB may approve, reject or ask for more detail.

Release windows are the agreed times when production changes may happen, for example Tuesday and Thursday evenings. Freeze periods are times when no changes are allowed, such as month-end for finance teams or the holiday season for retailers. Ask for the change calendar in week one. Many go-live dates slip because the team learns about a freeze or a CAB deadline too late.

Treat the CAB as an ally. Its questions (what if it fails, who can undo it) are the same ones you should be asking. A clear, short change request with tested rollback steps gets approved quickly and builds your reputation.
subtopics.example: Castlemere's CAB meets on Wednesdays and needs requests by Monday noon. Their freeze runs through the last three working days of each quarter, when bills are issued. The FDE learns this in week two and books go-live for Saturday 14 June, with the change request submitted on 2 June and approved on 4 June.

subtopics.title: Cutover plan, go/no-go and rollback
subtopics.body:
The cutover plan is a timed, step-by-step script for the switch. Each step has a number, a start time, an owner, the exact action, how to check it worked, and what to do if it fails. It is rehearsed at least once in staging. A good plan also names a decision point: the latest time you can still roll back without hurting the business.

Rollback means returning to the old way of working. Decide the rollback method before cutover and test it: switch a routing rule back, turn off a feature flag, or point users back to the old system. A rollback that has never been tested is a hope, not a plan. Some changes, such as a data migration that users start editing, get harder to reverse over time; that is why the decision point matters.

The go/no-go meeting happens shortly before cutover, often the day before and again at the start of the window. Each owner answers against the agreed criteria: UAT signed, change approved, dry run reconciled, rollback tested, runbook ready, support people named for the first week, users trained. The result is go, go with named risks accepted by the sponsor, or no-go with reasons and a new date. A no-go is not a failure; it is the process working.

During cutover, keep a live log with times and a single bridge call or chat channel. After the final checks pass, announce go-live to users with where to get help.
subtopics.example: At Castlemere, the go/no-go on Friday afternoon finds one open item: the runbook's escalation phone number is wrong. It is fixed in 20 minutes and the call ends with 'go'. Cutover runs from 07:00 to 10:40 on Saturday, reconciliation matches, and the decision point (11:00) passes without a rollback.

subtopics.title: The first week live: parallel run and hypercare
subtopics.body:
The first week after go-live is when real volume, real edge cases and real user habits appear. Two techniques reduce the risk.

A parallel run means the old process and the new system both run for a period, and you compare the results. For an AI router, agents might still triage manually while the AI's choice is recorded but not used, or the AI routes and a supervisor checks a sample against what they would have chosen. You agree an exit target in advance, for example 95% agreement over five working days, and review every difference. Parallel running costs effort, so keep it short and focused.

Hypercare is a period of extra support, usually two to six weeks, with the build team on hand, faster response targets, and a daily check-in with the customer. Define hypercare entry criteria before go-live: who is on call each day, which dashboards and alerts are live, where users report problems, how issues are triaged and how often you report status. Also define exit criteria (covered in the Support model topic): stable error rates, no open critical issues, and a support team trained to take over.

Watch for signals beyond errors. Are people using it, or quietly going back to the old way? Are some teams or types of item worse than others? A daily 15-minute review of a few numbers and ten random items catches most problems while they are still small.
subtopics.example: In Castlemere's first week, supervisors check the AI's choice on a sample of emails. On day two, agreement is 87.5% on the sample below; the difference is a billing email about a smart meter. The team adds three examples to the prompt and a rule for 'meter reading' wording. By day five agreement is 96%, and the service manager agrees to stop the parallel check.
checklist: On-call rota for every day of week one, with phone numbers
Dashboards and alerts live and tested
One place for users to report issues
Daily 15-minute review booked with the customer
Parallel-run exit target agreed in writing
Rollback still possible and owner named
Hypercare exit criteria written down

# Parallel run: the old process and the new system handle the same week
old = {"T-101": "billing", "T-102": "outage", "T-103": "billing",
       "T-104": "meter", "T-105": "outage", "T-106": "moving",
       "T-107": "billing", "T-108": "meter"}
new = {"T-101": "billing", "T-102": "outage", "T-103": "meter",
       "T-104": "meter", "T-105": "outage", "T-106": "moving",
       "T-107": "billing", "T-108": "meter"}

diffs = [t for t in old if old[t] != new.get(t)]
agree = 1 - len(diffs) / len(old)
print(f"agreement: {agree:.1%}")
for t in diffs:                      # every difference gets a human review
    print(t, "old:", old[t], "new:", new[t])

EXIT_TARGET = 0.95                   # agreed in the cutover plan
print("ready to stop the old process" if agree >= EXIT_TARGET
      else "keep running both; review the differences")

# Output:
# -> agreement: 87.5%
# -> T-103 old: billing new: meter
# -> keep running both; review the differences

glossary: Environment
A separate copy of a system (dev, test, staging or production) with its own servers, settings and data.
Staging
A pre-production environment set up like production, used to rehearse releases.
Data migration
Moving existing records from an old system to a new one.
Backfill
Processing historical data so a new system has useful history from day one.
Reconciliation
Proving with counts, totals and ID lists that migrated data matches the source.

Business users testing the system on realistic tasks and formally accepting it.
Defect triage

Agreed times when production changes are allowed.
Cutover

A short decision meeting before cutover where owners confirm agreed criteria are met.

supportops.plain: A support model is the agreed way a customer gets help once a system is live: who they contact, how problems are sorted by how serious they are, how fast each kind gets an answer, and who fixes what. Support is usually split into tiers. Level 1 (L1) answers common questions, Level 2 (L2) digs into harder problems such as configuration or data, and Level 3 (L3) is the engineering team that changes code. Escalation means passing a problem up to a tier or team that can solve it. Hypercare is the short period of extra support right after go-live, before the normal support model takes over.
supportops.analogy: It is like a hospital. The front desk answers simple questions and books you in (L1), a nurse examines you and handles most cases (L2), and a specialist surgeon is called only when needed (L3). A triage nurse decides how urgent each patient is, so a heart attack is not waiting behind a sprained ankle.
supportops.why: Job postings for FDEs often say 'own customer escalations'. After go-live, the FDE is frequently the person the customer calls first, and a messy support model burns the FDE's time and the customer's trust. Setting up tiers, severities and a clean handover lets the FDE move to the next project while the customer still gets fast, reliable help.

subtopics.title: Support tiers and where the FDE sits
subtopics.body:
Most software companies organise support into tiers so that simple questions are answered quickly and expensive engineers work only on problems that need them.

L1, first line, receives every request through a portal, email, chat or phone. L1 staff answer known questions from the knowledge base (password resets, 'how do I export'), collect the facts (who, what, when, screenshots, IDs) and log the ticket. They solve many tickets, often around half or more in mature teams. L2, second line, handles problems that need investigation: reading logs, checking configuration, reproducing the issue, fixing data. L3, third line, is usually the product engineering team; they fix bugs in code and ship patches. Some companies add L0, meaning self-service such as help articles and chatbots.

The customer often has its own help desk too. A common pattern is that the customer's IT service desk is L1 for their users, and your company provides L2 and L3. Write down this boundary clearly: which tickets the customer's help desk solves alone, and when they pass them to you.

Where does the FDE sit? During a deployment and hypercare, the FDE often acts as L2 and sometimes L3, because they know the customer's setup best. The goal is to move out of that role. Every ticket the FDE handles personally should result in a runbook entry or knowledge article so that L1 or L2 can handle the next one.
subtopics.example: Orrin Bay Pharmacy (made up, 220 stores) goes live with an AI assistant that answers staff questions about stock and policies. The pharmacy's own IT service desk is L1 for store staff. The vendor's support team is L2. The vendor's engineers are L3. For the first four weeks, the FDE joins L2 and reviews every ticket escalated past the service desk.

subtopics.title: Severity levels and response SLAs
subtopics.body:
Severity describes how badly a problem hurts the customer. Priority is how soon you will work on it; the two are usually linked but not always the same. A typical scale has four levels. Severity 1: the system is down or producing harmful results for many users, and there is no workaround. Severity 2: a major feature is broken or badly degraded, or a workaround is painful. Severity 3: a minor feature is broken or a reasonable workaround exists. Severity 4: a question, cosmetic issue or feature request.

A service level agreement (SLA) is a promise in the contract about response. The most common promises are first response time (how quickly a person acknowledges the ticket and starts work) and update frequency (how often the customer hears progress). Some contracts add resolution or workaround targets. Severity 1 is often covered 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, while lower severities count only business hours. Always read the actual contract; SLAs vary a lot.

Agree clear examples of each severity with the customer, specific to their system, because 'major' means different things to different people. For an AI system, include cases like 'answers are confidently wrong for a whole category' as severity 1 or 2, even though nothing is technically down.

Edge cases: customers who mark everything severity 1. Handle this politely by re-classifying against the agreed examples and explaining why, while still responding quickly. Also watch for tickets that start as severity 3 and grow; severity can go up as well as down.
subtopics.example: The code checks four Orrin Bay tickets against example first-response targets. The severity 2 ticket was answered after 2 hours 30 minutes against a 2-hour target, so it is breached. The open severity 3 ticket is past its due time and needs attention now. A weekly SLA report like this shows the team where it is slipping.
subtopics.code:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

# First-response targets per severity (example SLA, check your contract)
FIRST_RESPONSE = {1: timedelta(minutes=30), 2: timedelta(hours=2),
                  3: timedelta(hours=8), 4: timedelta(days=2)}

tickets = [  # id, severity, opened, first reply (None = no reply yet)
    ("T-311", 1, "2026-03-10 09:05", "2026-03-10 09:20"),
    ("T-312", 2, "2026-03-10 09:40", "2026-03-10 12:10"),
    ("T-313", 3, "2026-03-10 10:00", None),
    ("T-314", 4, "2026-03-09 16:00", "2026-03-10 11:00"),
]
now = datetime(2026, 3, 10, 19, 0)
fmt = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"

for tid, sev, opened, replied in tickets:
    due = datetime.strptime(opened, fmt) + FIRST_RESPONSE[sev]
    done = datetime.strptime(replied, fmt) if replied else None
    if done:
        state = "met" if done <= due else "BREACHED"
    else:
        state = "open, overdue" if now > due else "open, on time"
    print(tid, f"Sev{sev}", "due", due.strftime("%a %H:%M"), state)

# Output:
# -> T-311 Sev1 due Tue 09:35 met
# -> T-312 Sev2 due Tue 11:40 BREACHED
# -> T-313 Sev3 due Tue 18:00 open, overdue
# -> T-314 Sev4 due Wed 16:00 met

subtopics.title: Triage: reproducing a customer ticket fast
subtopics.body:
Triage is the first look at a ticket to decide severity, owner and next step. The fastest way to solve most tickets is to reproduce them: make the same problem happen yourself, on purpose. Once you can reproduce it, you can test a fix.

Start by collecting the facts, ideally through a ticket form so users do not have to guess. You need: who is affected (one user, one team, everyone), what they did step by step, what they expected, what happened instead, when it started, and identifiers such as the request ID, conversation ID or document name. For an AI system, the exact input, the output, and the version of the prompt or model are essential. Without a request ID you are searching logs blindly.

Then narrow it down. Did something change recently (a release, a new data file, a model version)? Is it every user or one? Every input or one type? Try the same input in staging. Check logs and traces for that request ID. For AI answers, check which documents were retrieved: many 'wrong answer' tickets are really 'wrong or old document' tickets.

If you cannot reproduce it, say so and ask one precise question rather than a long list. Keep the customer updated at the promised frequency even when you have nothing new; silence feels like being ignored. Write what you found in the ticket as you go, so if it escalates the next person does not start from zero.
subtopics.example: A store manager at Orrin Bay reports 'the assistant gave the wrong return policy'. The FDE asks for the conversation ID, finds it in the trace, and sees the retriever returned the 2025 policy file. The 2026 file was uploaded but not re-indexed. Reproduced in staging in 12 minutes, fixed by re-running the index job, and the ticket gets a knowledge article on 'answer uses old document'.
checklist: Who is affected: one user, a team, or everyone?
Exact steps, expected result and actual result
When did it start, and did anything change then?
Request, conversation or document ID
For AI: exact input, output, prompt and model version
Reproduced in staging? Yes or no, with notes
Severity set against the agreed examples
Next update time promised to the customer

subtopics.title: Escalating into your own engineering and product
subtopics.body:
Some problems need your company's engineers (L3) or product managers to change the product. How you escalate decides whether they act quickly or ignore it.

A good escalation is short and complete. It states the customer impact in numbers (how many users, what business effect), the severity, clear reproduction steps, what you already ruled out, the evidence (IDs, logs, screenshots) and what you need, by when. 'Customer X is unhappy, please look' gets ignored. 'Severity 2: 220 stores get the wrong return policy for 1 in 6 questions; reproduced in staging with steps below; root cause is the index job skipping files over 10 MB; need a fix or guidance by Thursday' gets attention.

Separate bugs from feature requests. A bug is the product not doing what it is documented to do. A feature request is something it was never built to do. Engineers handle bugs through the bug process; product managers weigh feature requests against other customers' needs. Mixing them makes both slower. When several customers hit the same gap, collect the evidence in one place so product can see the pattern; this is one of the most valuable things an FDE does for their own company.

Follow your company's escalation path and use it every time, even when you know an engineer personally. Side-channel requests hide work, skip priorities and fail when that person is on holiday. Finally, close the loop: tell the customer what was decided and when, even if the answer is 'not this quarter'.
subtopics.example: The FDE finds that Orrin Bay's index job skips files over 10 MB. She files an L3 bug with steps, logs and impact, and separately logs a feature request for 'automatic re-index on upload', noting two other customers asked for it. Engineering fixes the size limit in the next patch; the feature goes on the product roadmap.

subtopics.title: Knowledge base and ticket deflection
subtopics.body:
A knowledge base (KB) is a searchable set of short articles that answer common questions and describe known problems with their fixes. Deflection means a user finds the answer themselves, or L1 solves the ticket with a KB article, so it never reaches L2 or L3. Deflection is the cheapest way to improve support, because the fastest ticket is one that never has to be escalated.

Find what to write by counting. Tag every closed ticket with a root-cause category, then each month list the top categories. The top two or three usually make up a large share of tickets. Write one article for each, in the user's words: a title that matches what people type ('The assistant cites an old policy'), the symptom, the cause in one sentence, the fix steps, and when to raise a ticket instead. Keep articles short and date them.

Put the articles where people look: in the ticket form (suggest articles as the user types), in the product's help menu, and in the L1 team's scripts. For an AI assistant, you can also add the top answers to the assistant's own help responses.

Measure it. Track ticket volume per category before and after the article, and the share of tickets solved at L1. If a category does not drop, the article is either hard to find or wrong. Also watch for repeat tickets that point to a product problem; an article is a workaround, while the real fix may belong in the escalation queue.
subtopics.example: Orrin Bay's first month has 150 tickets. Password resets and export questions are 70% of them. The FDE writes two KB articles and adds them to the service desk script and the ticket form. The code estimates that if half of those two categories are deflected, 52 tickets (35%) are avoided next month.
subtopics.code:
from collections import Counter

# One month of closed tickets, tagged with a root-cause category
tickets = (["password reset"] * 64 + ["how do I export"] * 41 +
           ["wrong summary"] * 18 + ["slow response"] * 9 +
           ["integration error"] * 7 + ["other"] * 11)

counts = Counter(tickets)
total = len(tickets)
print("tickets this month:", total)
for cat, n in counts.most_common(3):          # the top 3 are KB candidates
    print(f"{cat:16} {n:3}  {n / total:.0%}")

# If a KB article deflects half of the top two categories next month:
deflected = (counts["password reset"] + counts["how do I export"]) // 2
print("tickets avoided:", deflected, f"({deflected / total:.0%})")

# Output:
# -> tickets this month: 150
# -> password reset    64  43%
# -> how do I export   41  27%
# -> wrong summary     18  12%
# -> tickets avoided: 52 (35%)

subtopics.title: Exiting hypercare and handing to support
subtopics.body:
Hypercare should end on purpose, not fade out. Without clear exit criteria, the FDE stays the customer's personal help desk for months, which is expensive and prevents the support team from learning the system.

Agree exit criteria at go-live, in writing. Typical criteria: no open severity 1 or 2 tickets; ticket volume stable or falling for two weeks; SLA targets met for two weeks; the top ticket categories have KB articles; the runbook covers every alert; the support team (yours and the customer's) has handled real tickets on its own, with the FDE only watching; and the customer's product owner agrees.

Plan the handover as a series of steps. First, the support team shadows the FDE on tickets. Then they handle tickets while the FDE reviews. Finally the FDE steps back to an escalation contact only. Transfer knowledge in writing: the environment map, integration details, known issues with workarounds, contacts on both sides, and the history of important decisions. Hold a short handover meeting with the customer where the support lead is introduced by name, so the customer knows who to call.

Edge case: the customer wants the FDE to stay. Explain that support will be faster and more reliable with a team than with one person who travels and takes holidays. Offer a scheduled check-in, for example monthly for a quarter, so the relationship continues without the FDE being the help desk.
subtopics.example: Orrin Bay's hypercare was planned for four weeks. By week four, ticket volume has fallen from 150 to 61 a month, there are no open severity 1 or 2 tickets, and support has handled two weeks of tickets with the FDE only reviewing. The service manager signs off, and the FDE moves to monthly check-ins.

incidents.plain: An incident is an unplanned event that is hurting real users now, or will soon: the system is down, very slow, or producing wrong or harmful results. Running an incident means organising people so the harm stops quickly, the customer is kept informed, the cause is found and fixed, and the team learns from it afterwards. In the field, the FDE is often the person closest to the customer when this happens, so they need to know the roles, the order of work and how to talk to the customer under pressure.
incidents.analogy: It is like a fire in a building. First someone raises the alarm and a fire chief takes charge. Everyone gets out safely before anyone studies why the fire started. Someone keeps the people outside informed. Only when the fire is out does an investigator find the cause, and the report focuses on fixing wiring and exits, not on blaming the person who plugged in the heater.
incidents.why: Customers judge a vendor less by whether something breaks (everything breaks sometimes) and more by how the vendor behaves when it does. A calm, well-run incident with clear, regular updates can actually increase trust. A chaotic one, where the customer learns about the problem from their own users and hears nothing for hours, can end the relationship. FDEs are expected to lead or support these moments at customer sites.

subtopics.title: Declaring an incident and naming roles
subtopics.body:
The first decision is whether something is an incident at all. A useful rule: if real users are affected now, or will be soon, and the normal ticket process is too slow, declare an incident. Declaring is cheap. You can downgrade the severity later or close it as a false alarm, but a late declaration wastes the most valuable minutes.

Declaring means a few concrete things: set a severity (using the same scale as your support model, for example Sev 1 to Sev 4), open a dedicated channel or call, start a written timeline, and tell the right people. Many teams use a short command in their chat tool that creates the channel automatically.

Next, name roles out loud. The incident commander (IC) coordinates: they decide what happens next, assign work and keep everyone focused. The IC does not debug; if the IC is buried in logs, nobody is watching the whole picture. The scribe writes the timeline with times: what was seen, what was tried, what was decided. The communications lead writes updates for the customer and internal leaders. Subject matter experts (engineers, the FDE, the customer's IT staff) investigate and fix.

In a small team one person may hold two roles, but say who holds each one. At a customer, agree who is the IC on each side. Often the customer's major incident manager runs their process and you are the lead for your product.

Edge case: if nobody is sure who is IC, the first person to declare is IC until they hand over explicitly: 'Priya, you now have command.'
subtopics.example: At Tollbury Mutual Insurance (made up), a claims handler phones at 09:45 to say the claims assistant shows errors. The FDE checks the dashboard: 30% of summaries are failing. She declares a Sev 2 at 09:48, opens a channel, names herself IC, asks a vendor engineer to investigate, and asks her colleague to act as scribe and comms lead.
