subtopics.title: Stabilise first: rollback, kill switch, feature flag
subtopics.body:
During an incident the first goal is to stop the harm, not to understand it. This is called mitigation or stabilising. Diagnosis can wait until users are safe, and it is much easier without pressure.

The main tools are prepared in advance. A rollback returns to the last version that worked, for example redeploying yesterday's release or restoring the previous prompt. A feature flag is a setting that turns one feature on or off without a new release, so you can switch off just the broken part. A kill switch is a flag that turns the whole AI path off and sends users to a safe fallback, often the manual process they used before. Other options are scaling up servers, blocking one bad input source, or pausing a batch job.

Ask three questions: what changed recently (a release, a prompt, a data feed, a config)? Can we undo it? What is the safest fallback for users? If a change happened just before the problem started, rolling it back is usually the fastest test and fix at once.

Edge cases matter. Rolling back code does not undo bad data already written; you may need to find and correct those records. Some changes cannot be rolled back, such as a database migration, which is why the cutover plan should include a rollback method (see the golive topic). And a kill switch that nobody has ever tested may itself fail, so test it in staging on a schedule.

When you mitigate, record the exact time in the timeline, then watch the metrics to confirm the harm has stopped.
subtopics.example: The code shows a simple kill switch. With the flag on, one claim containing a scanned PDF errors because the document service times out. When the IC flips the flag off, every claim goes to the manual queue users had before, so nobody sees an error while the team investigates.

subtopics.title: Customer communication cadence
subtopics.body:
Cadence means the rhythm of updates. Customers can accept a lot of bad news; what they cannot accept is silence. Good incident communication has three kinds of message.

The first notice goes out quickly, often within 15 to 30 minutes of declaring a Sev 1 or Sev 2. It says what you see, who is affected, what you are doing now, any workaround, who is leading, and when the next update will come. Do not guess at the cause in the first notice; say 'investigating'.

Updates go out on the promised timer, for example every 30 minutes for Sev 1 and every hour for Sev 2. Always include the time of the next update, and keep that promise even when nothing has changed: 'No change. We are testing a fix in staging. Next update 11:15.' An update that arrives on time with no news builds more trust than a perfect update an hour late.

The resolved notice confirms the end: start and end times, the impact, what fixed it, anything users need to do (such as resubmit failed items), and when the written review will arrive.

Write in plain language, avoid internal jargon, and use the customer's words for their systems. Use one channel the customer chose, such as their incident ticket, a status page or an email list, so updates are not scattered. Separate audiences if needed: an executive wants impact and time to recovery, while the IT team wants technical detail.

Edge case: if you miss an update, send one immediately and acknowledge it.
subtopics.example: Tollbury's IC promised updates every 30 minutes. The code checks the log of sent updates and finds one gap of 53 minutes, while the team was busy testing a fix. The review later adds a rule: the comms lead, not the engineers, owns the timer and sets a phone alarm.
subtopics.code:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

# Updates promised every 30 minutes for a Sev 1 (check your own contract)
CADENCE = timedelta(minutes=30)
fmt = "%H:%M"
sent = ["09:52", "10:20", "10:48", "11:41", "12:05"]   # times each customer update went out
resolved = "12:30"

times = [datetime.strptime(t, fmt) for t in sent] + [datetime.strptime(resolved, fmt)]
for before, after in zip(times, times[1:]):
    gap = after - before
    flag = "  MISSED (promised by " + (before + CADENCE).strftime(fmt) + ")" if gap > CADENCE else ""
    print(before.strftime(fmt), "->", after.strftime(fmt), int(gap.total_seconds() // 60), "min" + flag)

# Output:
# -> 09:52 -> 10:20 28 min
# -> 10:20 -> 10:48 28 min
# -> 10:48 -> 11:41 53 min  MISSED (promised by 11:18)
# -> 11:41 -> 12:05 24 min
# -> 12:05 -> 12:30 25 min

subtopics.title: Working in the customer's war room and ITSM process
subtopics.body:
Large customers have their own incident process, usually run in an IT service management (ITSM) tool such as a ticketing system with incident and change records. For a big outage they open a bridge: a conference call, sometimes a physical war room, run by their major incident manager. Your product is one part of their incident, and you are a guest in their process.

To work well inside it, learn the process before anything breaks. Find out during onboarding how they declare incidents, what their severity scale is (and how it maps to yours), who their major incident managers are, and how to join the bridge. Get access to their ITSM tool or agree who will update the ticket for you.

On the bridge, be short and structured. When asked for status, give: current impact, what you have done, what you are doing next, and when you will know more. Use their incident number in every message alongside your own ticket number, so both sides can find the records later. Do not argue about cause on the bridge; offer evidence and next steps.

Keep two tracks running. On their bridge you speak for your product. In your own internal channel your engineers debug, and your IC decides what to share. Someone must carry information between the two, often the FDE.

Edge case: during a customer incident, emergency changes may still need approval from their change process. Ask their incident manager how emergency changes are approved before you deploy a fix, even a rollback.
subtopics.example: At Tollbury, the customer's major incident manager opens bridge INC-40721 at 10:05. The FDE joins, gives a 30-second status, and adds the vendor ticket number to their record. She asks how an emergency rollback is approved and gets a verbal approval that the incident manager records in the ITSM tool.
checklist: Know their incident process and severity mapping before go-live
Names and numbers of their major incident managers
Access to their ITSM tool, or a named person who updates it
How to join their bridge, saved where on-call staff can find it
Emergency change approval route agreed
Both ticket numbers in every message
Status format: impact, done, next, next update time

subtopics.title: When the root cause is theirs, not yours
subtopics.body:
In the field, a large share of incidents are caused by something outside your product: an expired certificate on the customer's side, a firewall rule change, a new format in a data feed, a password rotated without notice, or a quota limit reached on a service they pay for. Your product broke, but the cause was theirs.

This is delicate. The customer's users see your product failing, so the customer may assume it is your fault. Their IT team may be defensive. Your job is to find the truth quickly and help fix it, without blame.

First, gather evidence before you speak: error messages, timestamps, and a clear line from their change to your failure. For example: 'Our calls to the document service started failing at 09:31 with a certificate error. Your change log shows a firewall update at 09:30.' Present it as a shared problem: 'It looks like the firewall change may be blocking our calls. Could your network team check rule 14?'

Second, help them fix it even though it is not your code. Offer the exact settings your product needs, test with them, and confirm recovery on your side.

Third, ask what you could do better too. Could your product have failed more gracefully, alerted earlier, or shown a clearer error? Almost every incident has contributing factors on both sides.

Edge case: sometimes you cannot prove the cause. Say what you know and do not know, and propose a test that would settle it.
subtopics.example: Tollbury's errors start one minute after a firewall update by their network team. The FDE shares the log line and the change time, their network engineer corrects the rule at 11:55, and summaries recover. The vendor's own action from this is to show a clear 'document service unreachable' message instead of a generic error.

subtopics.title: Running the blameless review and tracking actions
subtopics.body:
After the incident is resolved, the team writes a review, often called a post-incident review or post-mortem. The atlas has a post-mortem template; this subtopic is about running it well with a customer.

Blameless means the review assumes people acted reasonably with the information they had, and asks how the system let the failure happen. 'Raj changed the firewall' is blame. 'Firewall changes had no step to check dependent services' is a fixable cause. People who fear blame hide facts, and hidden facts cause the next incident.

A good review has: a summary in plain language, impact (who, how many, how long), a timeline from the scribe's notes, the root cause and contributing factors, what went well, and a short list of actions. Hold the meeting within a week while memories are fresh, and invite both sides when the customer was involved.

Actions are where most reviews fail. Each action needs one owner (a person, not a team), a due date and a way to check it is done. Prefer fewer, stronger actions: an alert, a test, a process step. 'Be more careful' is not an action. Put actions in a tracker and review them weekly until closed.

Share a customer version of the review. It is usually shorter, focuses on impact, cause and actions, and leaves out internal detail. Customers are often reassured by a clear, honest review.

Edge case: when an action belongs to the customer, you cannot force it. Record it, explain the risk, and follow up in your regular meetings.
subtopics.example: Tollbury's review lists four actions. Two weeks later the code shows only one is done and the customer's dashboard action is overdue. The FDE raises it in the weekly meeting with the IT manager rather than letting it quietly slip.
subtopics.code:
from datetime import date

# Actions from the blameless review, tracked until they are done
actions = [
    # action,                                        owner,          due,              done
    ("Alert when summary errors pass 5% for 5 min",   "Sam (vendor)",  date(2026, 4, 3),  True),
    ("Add document service health to the dashboard",  "Mia (customer)", date(2026, 4, 10), False),
    ("Test the kill switch in staging each month",     "Sam (vendor)",  date(2026, 4, 17), False),
    ("Tell the vendor before firewall changes",       "Raj (customer)", date(2026, 4, 24), False),
]
today = date(2026, 4, 14)

open_items = [a for a in actions if not a[3]]
print(f"{len(actions) - len(open_items)} of {len(actions)} actions done")
for text, owner, due, done in open_items:
    status = "OVERDUE" if due < today else f"due in {(due - today).days} days"
    print(f"- {text} | {owner} | {status}")

# Output:
# -> 1 of 4 actions done
# -> - Add document service health to the dashboard | Mia (customer) | OVERDUE
# -> - Test the kill switch in staging each month | Sam (vendor) | due in 3 days
# -> - Tell the vendor before firewall changes | Raj (customer) | due in 10 days

glossary: Incident
An unplanned event that is hurting users now, or soon will, and needs urgent coordinated work.
Declare
Formally start an incident: set severity, open a channel, start a timeline, name roles.
Incident commander (IC)
The person who coordinates the response and makes decisions, without debugging personally.
Scribe
The person who records a timed timeline of what was seen, tried and decided.
Mitigation
Actions that stop or reduce the harm quickly, before the cause is fully understood.
Rollback
Returning to the last known good version of code, configuration or prompt.
Feature flag
A setting that turns one feature on or off without a new release.
Kill switch
A flag that turns an entire feature off and sends users to a safe fallback.
Bridge or war room
A call or room where everyone working on a major incident meets.
ITSM
IT service management: the customer's processes and tool for incidents, changes and requests.
Status page
A web page where a vendor posts the current state of its service and incident updates.
Blameless review
A post-incident review that looks for system causes rather than people to blame.
Contributing factor
Something that did not cause the incident alone but made it worse or more likely.
practice: Write the first customer notice for this situation: since 14:10, your AI search tool returns no results for about half of a customer's staff. Include every part a first notice needs.
Change the cadence code so the promised gap depends on severity (30 minutes for Sev 1, 60 for Sev 2) and test it on a Sev 2 log with one 70-minute gap.
List three mitigations you could prepare in advance for an AI assistant you might deploy, and how you would test each one.
Rewrite these review actions so each has one owner, a date and a check: 'be more careful with releases', 'improve monitoring', 'talk to the customer more'.
Stretch: role-play a 20-minute incident with two friends (IC, comms lead, customer). Use a timer for updates and write the timeline as you go.

enablement.plain: Enablement means making the customer's people able to use, run and grow an AI system well on their own, long after the FDE leaves. It is broader than training: it includes the right skills for each group, materials based on their real work, help channels, internal champions, and a way to measure whether people can actually do their tasks better. An AI Center of Excellence (CoE) is a small internal team at the customer that owns AI standards, takes in new ideas and spreads what works across the organisation.
enablement.analogy: Think of teaching a town to swim rather than giving one swimming lesson. You train lifeguards (admins), swimming teachers (champions and builders) and ordinary swimmers (end users). You put up signs about where the water is deep (when to trust the output). You run weekly open sessions (office hours). And the town sets up a small pool committee (the CoE) that decides on new pools and safety rules.
enablement.why: Many AI deployments work technically but fail commercially because usage drops a few weeks after launch. The renewal, the next use case and the FDE's reputation all depend on adoption. The FDE is often the only person who knows both the system and the customer's daily work, so they are best placed to design enablement that sticks. This topic builds on the change topic (general change management and training plans) and focuses on what is specific to AI tools.

subtopics.title: Enablement versus training: admins, builders, end users
subtopics.body:
Training is one activity: a session where someone teaches. Enablement is the whole system that makes people capable: role-specific skills, materials, practice on real tasks, places to get help, and measurement of what people can do afterwards. You judge training by attendance; you judge enablement by behaviour weeks later.

Start by splitting the audience into groups, because each needs different things.

Admins run the system: they manage users and permissions, watch dashboards, update knowledge sources, handle first-line issues and follow the runbook. They need deep, hands-on sessions and the runbook itself.

Builders extend the system: they write and test new prompts, add documents, build small workflows or new use cases using approved patterns. They need to understand how the system works inside, how to evaluate changes before releasing them, and the CoE's standards.

End users use the tool in daily work. They need short, task-based learning: how to do their three most common tasks with the tool, how to check the output, and where to get help. Most of them do not need to know how the model works.

Also consider leaders, who need to know what good use looks like so they can encourage it and set expectations.

For each group, write the goal as a task they can do, not a topic they heard about. 'Can update the policy documents and confirm the assistant uses the new version' is a goal. 'Attended admin training' is not. Plan enablement early, alongside the build, not in the last week before go-live.
subtopics.example: Quillon Hart LLP (a made-up law firm with 600 staff) is rolling out a document assistant. The FDE plans for 3 admins in IT, 12 builders in the knowledge team, 480 end users (lawyers and assistants), and 20 partners who lead practice groups.

rows: Add prompts and use cases safely
Do top 3 tasks and check output
Use it weekly on real work

subtopics.title: Teaching users when to trust the output
subtopics.body:
The most important skill for an AI end user is calibrated trust: trusting the output as much as it deserves, no more and no less. Two failures are common. Over-trust (sometimes called automation bias) is accepting whatever the tool says, so errors slip into real work. Under-trust is refusing to use the tool or re-doing everything by hand, so there is no benefit.

Teach calibration with real examples from their work, not generic warnings. Show three cases where the tool is excellent and three where it fails, and explain the pattern. For example: summaries of long documents are good; exact numbers, dates and names must always be checked; questions about documents the tool has not been given will get confident but invented answers.

Then give each type of output a quick check that users can actually do in their workflow. The table below shows examples. Make checking easy by design: show sources and quotes next to answers, highlight numbers, and make 'report a bad answer' one click.

Set clear rules about where the tool must not be used, such as final legal advice without review, or decisions about individual people. Write these in the guide and repeat them in training.

Finally, make it normal to reject a bad answer. Users often think a wrong output is their fault. Tell them wrong outputs are expected sometimes, reporting them helps, and nobody will be blamed for spotting one.

Edge case: trust drifts over time. After weeks without errors, users stop checking. Short refreshers with fresh failure examples help.
subtopics.example: In Quillon Hart's end-user session, the FDE shows a lease summary where the assistant got the rent review date wrong by a year. Lawyers learn the rule 'every date gets checked against the clause' and the interface now shows the clause number next to each date.

rows: Do not use for client work

subtopics.title: Prompt libraries and worked examples from their own work
subtopics.body:
A prompt library is a shared, searchable collection of tested prompts for the organisation's real tasks. Each entry is more than the prompt text. A useful entry has: an ID, the task in plain words, the team, the prompt with clear placeholders (for example {text}), an example input and a good output, how to check the output, and who owns the entry. The prompting topic covers how to write good prompts; the library is how you share and maintain them.

Why build from their own work? Generic tips ('be specific', 'give context') are forgotten quickly. A worked example that shows a real (anonymised) lease, the exact prompt, and the output next to what a senior lawyer would write is memorable and immediately useful.

How to build one. First, collect the ten most common tasks from interviews and usage logs. Second, write and test a prompt for each on several real examples, fixing failures. Third, have a respected user from the team review each entry. Fourth, publish in the place people already work, such as a shared page, the tool's built-in templates or the intranet. Fifth, assign an owner and a review date, because models and tasks change.

Edge cases: many near-duplicate prompts (merge them and keep the best), prompts that include confidential example text (anonymise before publishing), and prompts that break after a model update (re-test the library when the model changes, using the evals approach from the evals topic).

The atlas includes a prompt-library template you can copy.
subtopics.example: The code stores two Quillon Hart library entries as simple records, finds the lease entry for the property team, fills in the placeholder and shows the check step. In practice this would live in the tool or on an intranet page, but the fields are the same.
subtopics.code:
# A tiny prompt library: each entry is a tested prompt for one real task
LIBRARY = [
    {"id": "LEASE-01", "task": "Summarise a lease for a client email", "team": "property",
     "prompt": "Summarise this lease in 5 bullet points for a client who is not a lawyer. "
               "Quote the clause number for each point. Lease: {text}",
     "check": "Open each quoted clause and confirm the bullet matches it"},
    {"id": "EMP-03", "task": "List dates and deadlines in a contract", "team": "employment",
     "prompt": "List every date and deadline in this contract as a table with clause numbers. {text}",
     "check": "Compare every date against the source; never trust a date you have not seen"},
]

def find(team, word):
    return [e for e in LIBRARY if e["team"] == team and word in e["task"].lower()]

entry = find("property", "lease")[0]
filled = entry["prompt"].format(text="[paste lease here]")
print(entry["id"], "|", entry["task"])
print(filled[:60] + "...")
print("Before you send:", entry["check"])

# Output:
# -> LEASE-01 | Summarise a lease for a client email
# -> Summarise this lease in 5 bullet points for a client who is ...
# -> Before you send: Open each quoted clause and confirm the bullet matches it

subtopics.title: Train-the-trainer and champions
subtopics.body:
An FDE cannot personally train 500 people, and even if they could, the knowledge would leave with them. Train-the-trainer solves this: the FDE trains a small group deeply, and they train everyone else. Champions are enthusiastic users inside each team who help colleagues, collect feedback and share tips. Often the same people are both trainers and champions.

Choosing champions. Look for people who are respected by their peers, curious about the tool, and good at explaining, not only the most senior or the most technical. Aim for roughly one champion per 15 to 30 users, with at least one in every team or site. Ask their managers to protect some of their time, for example two hours a week for the first two months, and recognise the role in their goals.

Preparing them. Give champions more than users get: deeper sessions, early access, the prompt library, known issues and workarounds, the escalation route for bugs, and a ready-made training kit (slides, exercises from their team's work, a facilitator guide). Have each champion co-teach one session with the FDE before they teach alone.

Keeping them going. Run a champions channel and a short monthly call to share questions and tips. Feed their feedback into fixes and new library entries, and tell them what changed because of it. Champions who see no effect stop contributing.

Edge cases: a champion leaves (keep at least two per large team), or a champion spreads a bad habit (review their materials and correct gently in the monthly call).
subtopics.example: Quillon Hart picks 24 champions across 8 practice groups. The FDE runs three deep sessions, then each champion co-teaches with her once. Within six weeks, champions have run 31 sessions for 430 users, and the FDE has taught only 4 herself.
checklist: One champion per 15 to 30 users, at least one per team
Manager agrees protected time in writing
Deeper training plus early access
Training kit with exercises from their own team
Co-teach one session before teaching alone
Champions channel and monthly call
Show champions what changed from their feedback
Backup champion for each large team

subtopics.title: Standing up the Center of Excellence: roles and intake
subtopics.body:
A Center of Excellence (CoE) for AI is a small, cross-functional group inside the customer that owns how AI is used across the organisation. The arc topic mentions the CoE as a phase goal; this subtopic is about how to set one up.

What it does. A CoE usually has four jobs: intake (collecting and reviewing new AI ideas), standards (approved tools, data rules, review and evaluation steps, the prompt library), enablement (training, champions, office hours), and reporting (what was approved, what value it delivered, what was learned).

Who is in it. Keep it small: a lead with real protected time (ideally at least half their week), a technical owner from IT or data, a representative from security or risk, and two or three people from the business. Legal and privacy join for reviews that need them. The FDE often helps design the CoE and attends its first meetings, then steps back.

Intake. Make it easy to submit an idea with a short form: the problem, who benefits, what data it uses, and who sponsors it. Review ideas on a regular schedule, for example every two weeks, using a simple, published scoring rubric (the aireadiness topic covers use-case scoring). Routing rules keep reviews fast: ideas that reuse an approved pattern and use no sensitive data get a fast track; ideas that affect individual people get a full review.

Edge cases: a CoE with a charter but no owner, budget or intake process becomes a monthly meeting with no output. A CoE that only says no drives people to use tools secretly. Publish decisions and reasons.
subtopics.example: Quillon Hart's CoE uses these routing rules. The code shows four submitted ideas: two go to the fast track, the staff-resignation prediction goes to full review because it makes decisions about individual people, and the canteen chatbot has no sponsor yet.
subtopics.code:
# CoE intake: route each new idea by a few simple rules
ideas = [
    {"name": "Draft replies to billing emails", "personal_data": True,  "approved_pattern": True,  "sponsor": True},
    {"name": "Summarise board papers",          "personal_data": False, "approved_pattern": True,  "sponsor": True},
    {"name": "Predict which staff will resign", "personal_data": True,  "approved_pattern": False, "sponsor": True},
    {"name": "Chatbot for the canteen menu",    "personal_data": False, "approved_pattern": False, "sponsor": False},
]

def route(i):
    if not i["sponsor"]:
        return "Return: find a business sponsor first"
    if i["personal_data"] and not i["approved_pattern"]:
        return "Full review: security, legal and ethics"
    if i["personal_data"]:
        return "Fast track + privacy check"
    return "Fast track: use approved pattern"

for i in ideas:
    print(f'{i["name"]:32} {route(i)}')

# Output:
# -> Draft replies to billing emails  Fast track + privacy check
# -> Summarise board papers           Fast track: use approved pattern
# -> Predict which staff will resign  Full review: security, legal and ethics
# -> Chatbot for the canteen menu     Return: find a business sponsor first

subtopics.title: Office hours, communities and measuring skill growth
subtopics.body:
After launch, people need easy, ongoing help. Office hours are regular open sessions, often 30 to 60 minutes weekly, where anyone can drop in with questions or bring real work to try with an expert. A community is a shared space, such as a chat channel, where users ask questions, share prompts and see what others do. Both lower the cost of asking for help, which is the main barrier after the first training.

Keep them useful: announce a topic each week but welcome any question, have a champion or CoE member answer channel questions within a day, and turn repeated questions into library entries or help articles.

Measuring skill growth. Attendance and satisfaction scores are easy to collect but do not show whether people got better. Use a mix of measures. A task check: the same short practical exercise before training and some weeks after, scored against a rubric. Usage: the share of people using the tool at least weekly, per team, and whether they use it for the target tasks. Quality: the rate of reported bad answers that were caught before reaching clients, or reviewer scores on outputs. Outcome: time saved or turnaround on the target tasks, linked to the business case.

Look at results per team, not only in total, because averages hide teams that are stuck. A team with low usage and little score growth needs a conversation, not more of the same training. Often the cause is a task mismatch or a manager who does not support it.

Edge case: usage can be high while quality is poor. Always pair usage with a quality check.
subtopics.example: Six weeks after Quillon Hart's training, the code compares task-check scores and weekly use per team. Litigation barely improved and only 20% use the tool weekly. The FDE learns in office hours that litigation's main task, reviewing large evidence bundles, is not supported well, and brings the gap to the CoE.
subtopics.code:
# Skill growth: same 10-question task check before training and 6 weeks later,
# plus the share of each team using the tool at least weekly
teams = {
    # team:        (score before, score after, weekly users, team size)
    "Property":    (4.1, 7.8, 34, 40),
    "Employment":  (3.8, 7.2, 22, 30),
    "Litigation":  (4.3, 4.9,  9, 45),
}
for name, (before, after, users, size) in teams.items():
    active = users / size
    note = "  <- follow up" if after - before < 1 or active < 0.5 else ""
    print(f"{name:11} score {before} -> {after} (+{after - before:.1f})  weekly use {active:.0%}{note}")

# Output:
# -> Property    score 4.1 -> 7.8 (+3.7)  weekly use 85%
# -> Employment  score 3.8 -> 7.2 (+3.4)  weekly use 73%
# -> Litigation  score 4.3 -> 4.9 (+0.6)  weekly use 20%  <- follow up

glossary: Enablement
The whole system that makes people capable of using a tool well: skills, materials, help, measurement.
End user
A person who uses the tool in their daily work without changing how it works.
Builder
A customer staff member who extends the system, for example by adding prompts or use cases.
Calibrated trust
Trusting an AI output as much as it deserves, checking the parts that are often wrong.
Automation bias
The tendency to accept a computer's output without checking it.
Prompt library
A shared collection of tested prompts for real tasks, each with an example, a check and an owner.
Train-the-trainer
Training a small group deeply so they can train everyone else.
Champion
A respected user in a team who helps colleagues, collects feedback and shares good practice.
Center of Excellence (CoE)
A small cross-functional group that owns AI intake, standards, enablement and reporting.
Intake
The process for submitting and reviewing new ideas for AI use.
Office hours
Regular open sessions where anyone can bring questions or real work to an expert.
Task check
A short practical exercise scored before and after training to measure skill growth.
practice: Pick a tool you use at work or school. Write one goal for admins, builders and end users as a task each can do, and how you would check it.
Write a trust table for an AI tool you know: five output types, how far to trust each, and a quick check a busy user could do.
Write two prompt library entries for real tasks, with every field: ID, task, team, prompt with placeholders, example, check, owner.
Change the skill-growth code to also flag any team whose after-score is below 6, and add a fourth team to test it.
Stretch: draft a one-page CoE charter for a 600-person organisation: jobs, members and time, intake form fields, routing rules, and what it reports each quarter.
